idiom_name: one function per rule over a token slice, Result + ? for positioned errors
implementation_notes: Rust's enums, pattern matching and the ? operator make the hand-written parser clean but do not remove it: a token enum (usually with spans), a parser struct holding the slice and an index, one function per rule returning Result<Node, ParseError>, and peek/bump/expect helpers; errors are ordinary values with spans, so a rule fails without unwinding. What replaces the classic structure is the type system rather than a library: the token enum plus exhaustive match is the dispatch, Result is the error path, and the borrow checker forces the cursor design (indices into a slice or a separate token iterator). Keep this form when the grammar is yours, when diagnostics and recovery matter and when dependencies should stay small; pick a combinator variant when the grammar is better declared than coded.
pitfalls: Rust has no guaranteed tail-call elimination and stack overflow aborts the process instead of unwinding, so recursive rules need an explicit depth limit for untrusted input.

Borrowing the token slice immutably while mutating the position works only while the cursor is an index; returning references into the input from rules that also mutate shared state fights the borrow checker - choose indices or an owned token stream deliberately.

Result-based errors lose recovery information: decide early whether a rule aborts on the first error or collects diagnostics, and give the error type spans so messages can point at the offending token.

variants.name: nom parser combinators
variants.idiom_name: nom IResult functions composed with alt/opt/many0/delimited
variants.implementation_notes: nom is a parser combinator library focused on safe parsing, streaming and zero-copy: a parser is a function from input to IResult (the remaining input plus the output, or a nom error), and rules are composed from combinators such as tag, take_while, alt, opt, many0 and delimited, or written imperatively with ? inside a function. Choose it when the grammar is a pipeline of small recognisers over bytes or &str and zero-copy slices into the input are wanted; the cost is combinator type noise (mitigated by impl Parser and boxing) and error types that must be shaped by hand.
pitfalls: nom errors are values with an ErrorKind and an input position, not messages: user-facing diagnostics need a custom error type implementing ParseError and a conversion step.

Combinators consume input positionally, so a parser that returns a borrowed slice cannot also stream incrementally without the streaming variants; mixing streaming and complete submodules is a classic bug source.

variants.name: pest PEG grammar (.pest file)
variants.implementation_notes: pest compiles a PEG grammar written in its own .pest syntax into a parser via pest_derive: rules are declarative (expr = { term ~ ("+" | "-") ~ term }), whitespace and comments are handled by the WHITESPACE/COMMENT special rules, atomic rules suppress them for lexeme-like rules, and PUSH/POP/PEEK match delimiters using a stack. Choose it when the grammar should live in a grammar file with tooling (the pest fiddle, grammar analysis) and ordered choice plus unlimited lookahead is acceptable; the cost is a derive macro, a second language for the grammar, and a pair stream to walk instead of an AST you control.
pitfalls: The generated pair stream is a flat token-pair sequence, not an AST: building typed nodes means writing a walker over Pairs, and getting the nesting wrong is the common failure.
WHITESPACE and COMMENT are implicit in non-atomic rules, so a grammar that forgets atomic rules for keywords ends up accepting whitespace inside tokens it should reject.
